results.result: A novel bimanual stick manipulation task was developed where 72 participants manipulated a virtual stick (40 cm length, 15 cm hand separation) to reach targets with the stick tip. The task is kinematically redundant because the same tip position can be achieved with different stick angles, allowing investigation of both end-effector relevant (tip position) and end-effector irrelevant (stick-tilt angle) perturbations.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C37-C47, and C176-C184 provide comprehensive methodological details including participant demographics (N=72, right-handed, aged 22.1±2.5 years), apparatus specifications (KINARM system, sampling at 1 kHz), and task parameters (stick dimensions, target distances, velocity feedback). The redundancy of the task is clearly established both conceptually and through the experimental design.

results.result: During baseline movements, participants consistently adopted a stereotypical strategy where stick-tilt angle was significantly modulated by tip-movement direction (|t(71)|>5.5, p<0.01), establishing a baseline TMD-STA relationship. This strategy minimized hand movement distance to near-optimal levels (Cohen's d=1.914 vs. parallel translation, d=0.334 vs. theoretical minimum), with clockwise tip movements accompanied by clockwise stick-tilt and vice versa.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C48-C59, and C114-C122 are well-supported by statistical analyses (t-tests with Bonferroni correction, effect size calculations) and kinematic measurements shown in Figures 2-3. The stereotypical relationship is demonstrated from the first trials (C52) and quantified with appropriate statistical rigor. The optimization interpretation (C56, C119-C120) is supported by the distance minimization data.

results.result: In Experiment 1A (N=19), gradual 30° CCW tip-movement direction perturbation (1°/trial) led to implicit adaptation where participants corrected tip-movement direction (remained at baseline: t(18)=-1.320, p=0.203) by tilting the stick significantly more CW (t(18)=10.003, p<0.01). The adapted physical movement pattern followed the baseline TMD-STA relationship, resembling voluntary aiming at -30° target, with individual differences in stick-tilt correlated between baseline and adapted patterns (R=0.601, p=0.007).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C72, C115, C129-C130, and C185-C187 are supported by appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, correlation analysis) and data shown in Figures 4-5. The gradual perturbation protocol ensured implicit adaptation (C62, C187). The finding that adaptation followed the baseline relationship is demonstrated both qualitatively (Figure 5b-c) and quantitatively (C69-C70, C72), though a small but significant difference in tip-movement direction was noted (C69).

results.result: Experiment 1B (N=13) with abrupt 30° tip perturbation allowing explicit strategy produced nearly identical results to Experiment 1A, but without the significant difference in tip-movement direction observed in Experiment 1A when comparing adapted pattern to baseline -30° target aiming.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 and C188 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplements 2-3. The comparison between gradual (1A) and abrupt (1B) perturbation conditions provides important control data, though the sample size for 1B (N=13) is smaller than 1A (N=19). The absence of tip-movement direction difference in 1B (C75) contrasts with 1A (C74) and is appropriately documented.

results.result: The authors speculate that the residual tip-movement direction difference in Experiment 1A (but not 1B) was caused by implicit adaptation attempting to correct the abnormal visual stick-tilt angle, which would interfere with tip adaptation due to the baseline TMD-STA relationship constraint.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 and C144-C145 are explicitly labeled as speculation by the authors. While the speculation is logical given the baseline TMD-STA relationship, it is not directly tested in Experiment 1. The authors indicate that Experiments 2 and 3 provide support (C145), but this remains an interpretation rather than a directly demonstrated mechanism.

results.result: In Experiment 2 (N=20), end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt perturbations (±6° around tip) that did not affect tip position were applied. Contrary to minimal intervention principle predictions, participants corrected stick-tilt angle from early adaptation (main effect of perturbation direction: F(1,18)=12.483, p<0.01), though not fully compensating for the perturbation (stick-tilt remained different from baseline: F(1,18)=54.457, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C89 and C189-C192 are supported by appropriate two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs comparing E2CCW and E2CW groups across trial phases. The statistical analyses properly test main effects and interactions. The finding contradicts minimal intervention principle (C83, C146) and is clearly demonstrated in Figure 7a-b. The perturbation magnitude (±6°) was appropriately chosen based on baseline data (C80).

results.result: Stick-tilt correction in Experiment 2 was accompanied by undesirable tip-movement directional errors (main effect: F(1,18)=5.104, p=0.037). These errors were consistent with predictions from the baseline TMD-STA relationship: CCW/CW stick-tilt adaptation shifted tip-movement in CCW/CW direction. Participants with shallower baseline TMD-STA relationships showed greater stick-tilt correction (R=-0.572, p<0.01), though correlation with tip-movement change was not significant (R=-0.440, p=0.052).
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 and C155-C158 are supported by statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA, correlation analyses) and data in Figure 7c-f. The finding that end-effector irrelevant adaptation produces end-effector relevant errors is novel and counterintuitive (C90, C155). The correlation analyses (C93-C94, C158) appropriately test individual differences, though one correlation approaches but does not reach significance (C94).

results.result: The combined results of Experiments 1 and 2 suggest implicit adaptation in the redundant task operates through two mechanisms: (1) the motor system attempts to correct any visual feedback perturbation regardless of end-effector relevance, and (2) physical movement correction patterns are constrained by the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C95 and C116 synthesize findings from Experiments 1 and 2. The first mechanism is supported by Experiment 2 showing adaptation to end-effector irrelevant perturbations (C85-C89). The second mechanism is supported by both experiments showing adaptation trajectories following the baseline relationship (C68, C92). This synthesis is logical and well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: Experiment 3 (N=20) investigated interactions between end-effector relevant and irrelevant perturbations by simultaneously applying CCW tip perturbation with either CCW (E3CCW, N=10) or CW (E3CW, N=10) stick-tilt perturbation. The E3CCW combination was predicted to align with baseline TMD-STA relationship enabling smooth adaptation, while E3CW was predicted to be orthogonal to the relationship potentially preventing smooth adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 and C193-C195 describe the experimental design and predictions for Experiment 3. The design logically tests the interaction hypothesis derived from Experiments 1 and 2. The predictions (C98-C99) are clearly stated and based on the baseline TMD-STA relationship. Sample sizes are balanced between groups (N=10 each).

results.result: Contrary to predictions, final adapted movement patterns in Experiment 3 did not differ significantly between E3CCW and E3CW groups (tip-movement: t(18)=-0.479, p=0.638; stick-tilt: t(18)=-0.386, p=0.704). However, adaptation processes differed: trial-dependent trajectories were clearly separated (MANOVA group effect: F(8,162)=0.155, p<0.001), with E3CW showing more delayed tip-movement adaptation (trial segment 2: t(18)=-3.684, p<0.05). Trial-by-trial variability in latter adaptation phase also differed between groups (stick-tilt: t(18)=-3.235, p=0.005).
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106, C117, and C160 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (paired t-tests, repeated-measures MANOVA) shown in Figure 9. The finding that final patterns converged despite different trajectories is clearly demonstrated (C101-C102). The MANOVA appropriately tests multivariate effects across trial segments (C105). The delayed adaptation in E3CW (C106) supports the hypothesis that perturbation combinations affect adaptation dynamics even if final states converge.

results.result: The motor system's response to end-effector irrelevant perturbations (Experiment 2) is interpreted as predicting visual feedback of stick-tilt angle and attempting to eliminate dissociation between observed and predicted angles (sensory prediction error). This may reflect attempts to resolve vision-proprioception dissociation or utilize stick-tilt information to improve tip-movement direction estimation, given the tight coupling in the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C149 and C163-C168 present interpretations and speculations about mechanisms. While C146-C148 are supported by Experiment 2 data, the mechanistic explanations (C163-C168) are explicitly speculative. The sensory prediction error framework (C147) and multisensory integration perspective (C167-C168) are plausible but not directly tested. These remain interpretations rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

results.result: The baseline TMD-STA relationship plays a crucial role in both controlling movement of the redundant system and in how the motor system implicitly adapts to modify movement patterns. This relationship, developed through optimization, dictates physical control and informs visual feedback expectations. When perturbations occur, the motor system attempts to eliminate dissociations, but correction patterns are physically constrained by the baseline relationship, biasing adaptations toward this stereotypical relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C169-C175 synthesize the main conclusions across all experiments. The dual role of the baseline relationship (control and adaptation) is well-supported by baseline data (Figures 2-3) and adaptation experiments (Figures 5, 7, 9). The constraint on adaptation patterns is demonstrated across all three experiments. The framework (C175) integrating these findings is logical and supported by the data, though some mechanistic details remain interpretive.

results.result: The study addresses gaps in motor adaptation research by investigating redundant systems. Traditional non-redundant tasks (e.g., planar reaching) cannot examine how the motor system adapts by altering redundant body movement patterns. Previous studies on task-irrelevant perturbations applied perturbations to the end-effector, not to the redundant body while leaving the end-effector unaffected. The current study introduces a novel approach to investigate three problems: (1) coordinating redundant movements for end-effector control, (2) modifying redundant movements during adaptation to end-effector perturbations, and (3) responding to perturbations of redundant dimensions that don't affect the end-effector.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C36 and C107-C128 establish the background, motivation, and novelty of the study. The characterization of traditional approaches (C1-C2, C16-C21) is accurate and well-cited. The identification of gaps (C3, C27, C32, C126-C128) is appropriate. The distinction between previous "task-irrelevant" perturbations and the current "end-effector irrelevant" perturbations (C35-C36, C111-C112) is clearly articulated and represents a genuine conceptual advance.

results.result: The bimanual stick manipulation task has several advantages: it creates redundancy naturally using a familiar everyday action (manipulating a stick with both hands), as evidenced by participants tilting the stick from the beginning of the experiment. The task allows investigation of how tip-movement direction perturbations lead to changes in both tip-movement and stick-tilt angle.
results.evaluation: Claims C113, C123-C125 describe advantages of the experimental design. The familiarity claim (C123-C124) is supported by Figure 2f showing immediate stick-tilting behavior. The acknowledgment of limited generalizability (C113) is appropriate given the specific configuration tested. The task's capability to investigate coupled changes (C125) is demonstrated throughout the experiments.

results.result: The finding that baseline movement patterns guide implicit adaptation is consistent with Hayashi et al., 2016, who showed that distorting the visuomotor map affected adaptation magnitude. The residual errors observed in visuomotor adaptation have been attributed to imbalance between learning and forgetting, though recent work (Albert et al., 2021) suggests the implicit learning system modulates error sensitivity based on error consistency.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 and C141-C143 appropriately contextualize findings within prior literature. The comparison to Hayashi et al., 2016 (C133-C135) is apt and accurately represents that work. The discussion of residual errors (C141-C143) correctly cites relevant literature, though the connection to the current findings could be more explicit.

results.result: The adaptation pattern in Experiment 1A appears consistent with the minimal intervention principle because participants ignored abnormal visual stick-tilt that didn't directly influence the task. However, the difference between Experiments 1A and 1B implies a violation of this principle.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 and C67 present conflicting interpretations about the minimal intervention principle. While C67 and C139 suggest consistency with the principle, C140 suggests violation. The evidence from Experiment 2 (C146) more clearly contradicts the minimal intervention principle. This apparent inconsistency reflects the complexity of the findings but could be more clearly resolved in the manuscript.

results.result: Previous studies created "task-irrelevant" conditions by manipulating cursor trajectory, target/cursor shape, or applying simultaneous perturbations to target and cursor, which are not "end-effector irrelevant" as defined in the current study. While some studies (Dimitriou et al., 2012; Omrani et al., 2013) used end-effector irrelevant perturbations in postural tasks, such perturbations have not been used to investigate motor adaptation patterns in redundant systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C154 appropriately distinguish the current approach from previous work. The characterization of previous "task-irrelevant" manipulations (C150) is accurate and well-cited. The clarification that these are not "end-effector irrelevant" (C151) is conceptually important. The acknowledgment of exceptions (C152) and identification of the gap (C153) are appropriate.

results.result: Results from Experiment 3 support the existence of interaction between tip-movement and stick-tilt adaptation. If the motor system simply corrected stick-tilt to reduce sensory prediction error, the spillover effect on tip-movement would not have been observed. The motor system likely attempts to reduce both sensory prediction error and motor cost, given that the baseline TMD-STA relationship reflects motor cost minimization.
results.evaluation: Claims C159, C161-C162 present interpretations of Experiment 3 results. The interaction between adaptation types (C159) is supported by the separated trajectories and differential adaptation rates (C104-C106). The inference about dual optimization (C162) is logical given the baseline relationship reflects cost minimization (C119-C120), though this remains an interpretation rather than directly tested mechanism.

results.result: Data were analyzed using MATLAB R2023a with 10 Hz low-pass filtering (fourth-order Butterworth). Tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle were calculated relative to horizontal, with positive values indicating CCW direction. Values at peak tip velocity were used to evaluate feedforward motor commands. Statistical analyses included t-tests, correlations, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, and MANOVA.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C202 describe data analysis methods. Software and filtering parameters are specified (C196-C197). Variable definitions are clear (C198-C200). The choice to use peak velocity values (C201) is appropriate for assessing feedforward commands. Statistical methods (C202) are appropriate for the experimental designs, though more details about multiple comparison corrections would strengthen reproducibility.

results.result: The authors developed a novel bimanual stick manipulation task where participants manipulated a virtual stick held with both hands to reach targets with the stick tip. This task creates redundancy because the same tip position can be achieved with different stick angles, allowing investigation of both end-effector relevant (tip position) and end-effector irrelevant (stick angle) perturbations.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the novel task design. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors have developed a novel bimanual task that allows them to study how the sensorimotor control system deals with redundancy' and notes it 'provides a very fruitful and important framework.' Reviewer 3 calls it 'an innovative bimanual stick manipulation task' and Reviewer 1 describes it as 'a new task offering a myriad of possible coordination patterns.' The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing.'

results.result: During baseline movements, participants consistently employed a stereotypical strategy where stick-tilt angle was modulated by tip-movement direction, creating a baseline TMD-STA (tip-movement direction to stick-tilt angle) relationship. This relationship constrained movement patterns and was achieved by minimizing hand movement distance to near-optimal levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these baseline findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes 'findings are original and exemplify how baseline relationships determine learning.' Reviewer 2 states participants 'change the tilt angle of the stick in a specific pattern that produces close to minimum movement of the two hands.' The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing, as demonstrated over four different experiments.'

results.result: In Experiment 1, when tip-movement direction was perturbed (30° CCW rotation), participants adapted by changing both tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle. The adaptation followed the baseline TMD-STA relationship, with the adapted pattern resembling voluntary aiming at the -30° target. Individual differences in baseline stick-tilt predicted adapted stick-tilt magnitude.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as demonstrating that 'baseline relationships determine learning' (Reviewer 1). Reviewer 2 notes 'adaptation follows the baseline pattern of tip-movement and stick angle relation.' However, Reviewer 1 requests 'the time course of sensorimotor adaptation' be shown more clearly, suggesting presentation could be improved but not questioning the core findings.

results.result: In Experiment 2, when only stick-tilt angle was perturbed (±6° around the tip, leaving tip position unchanged), participants still adapted by correcting stick-tilt angle. Unexpectedly, this adaptation was accompanied by undesirable tip-movement direction errors, consistent with the constraint imposed by the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found this a key novel finding. Reviewer 2 notes 'even task-irrelevant perturbations drive adaptation in a manner that results in task-relevant errors,' calling this 'an important demonstration.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'the nervous system reacts to both types of perturbation' but requests more discussion of 'why adaptation was found in the experiments with end-effector irrelevant' perturbations and how internal models may explain this.

results.result: The study concludes that implicit adaptation in redundant systems is achieved by two mechanisms: (1) the motor system attempts to correct any perturbation in visual feedback regardless of task relevance, and (2) physical movement correction patterns are constrained by the baseline TMD-STA relationship. This relationship plays a crucial role in both controlling and adapting movements of redundant systems.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this as a valuable theoretical contribution. The editor states this is 'a valuable finding on how the sensorimotor control system deals with redundancy.' Reviewer 1 notes findings 'exemplify how baseline relationships determine learning.' Reviewer 2 calls it 'an important demonstration that underlying solutions/relations can affect the manner in which we adapt.' However, Reviewer 1 suggests 'the authors may consider modifying the last sentence of the abstract to clearly provide the most substantial theoretical advance.'

results.result: In Experiment 3, when both tip-movement and stick-tilt perturbations were applied simultaneously, the final adapted movement patterns were similar between groups regardless of stick-tilt perturbation direction. However, adaptation processes differed: tip-movement adaptation was more delayed when the required correction pattern was orthogonal to (rather than aligned with) the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as supporting the role of baseline relationships in adaptation. Reviewer 2 notes the work 'provides an important demonstration that underlying solutions/relations can affect the manner in which we adapt.' The editor confirms evidence is 'convincing, as demonstrated over four different experiments.' No reviewer challenged the Experiment 3 findings specifically.

results.result: Experiment 1B (abrupt 30° perturbation allowing explicit strategy) produced nearly identical results to Experiment 1A (gradual perturbation, implicit only), except that the small residual difference in tip-movement direction observed in 1A was absent in 1B. The authors speculate this difference reflects implicit correction of abnormal stick-tilt in Experiment 1A.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions whether 'all the necessary evidence appears in this study that control and adaptation are exclusively implicit' and notes 'there is no clear comparison between gradual and abrupt sessions.' The reviewer suggests 'the authors may consider removing at least from the title and abstract the words 'implicit' and 'implicitly.'' This indicates uncertainty about the implicit/explicit distinction and its interpretation.

results.result: The authors interpret their findings in relation to the minimal intervention principle, suggesting that while Experiment 1 results initially appear consistent with this principle (ignoring task-irrelevant stick-tilt errors), Experiment 2 results contradict it. They propose the motor system corrects end-effector irrelevant errors because: (1) it predicts all sensory consequences and corrects discrepancies, and/or (2) coupled dimensions mean irrelevant errors imply relevant errors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the nervous system reacts to both types of perturbation, indicating that they both seem relevant or important' and requests the authors 'extend the Discussion on why adaptation was found in the experiments with end-effector irrelevant and especially how an internal (forward) model or a pair of internal (forward) models may be used to predict both the visual and the somatosensory consequences.' This suggests the theoretical interpretation needs strengthening.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that experiments were conducted with a specific configuration (stick length, hand distance, target location) and caution about generalizability to other configurations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly raises this concern: 'The generalizability of the findings is limited. Future work may strengthen the present study's findings by examining whether the observed relationships hold for different stick lengths...or when reaching targets to the left and right of the starting position.' The editor notes 'further investigation into the interpretation of the findings could increase the generalisation of the study to a broader audience.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on Experiment 3 findings (C101-C106, C117, C160). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing that baseline relationships constrain adaptation patterns, with OpenEval providing detailed statistical validation and peer reviewers accepting these findings as supporting the theoretical framework.

Strong agreement on baseline stereotypical relationship findings (C5, C48-C59, C114, C119-C120). Both find the evidence well-supported through statistical analyses and kinematic data. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor while peer reviewers accept findings without challenge, noting the optimization interpretation.

Agreement on Experiment 1 adaptation findings (C63-C72, C115, C129-C130). Both accept that adaptation follows baseline relationships. Peer Reviewer 1 requests clearer presentation of time course data, suggesting presentation improvements rather than questioning core findings, while OpenEval finds evidence fully supported.

Strong agreement on task design and methodology (C4, C37-C46, C123-C125). All peer reviewers explicitly praised the novel task design as innovative and fruitful. OpenEval confirms comprehensive methodological documentation. Both evaluations find this aspect well-supported.

Agreement on main theoretical conclusions (C11-C12, C174-C175). Both find the dual role of baseline relationships (control and adaptation) to be a valuable theoretical contribution. Peer Reviewer 1 suggests clarifying the abstract's final sentence for theoretical impact, while OpenEval notes some mechanistic details remain interpretive.

Partial overlap on Experiment 2 findings. OpenEval R6 addresses statistical validation of end-effector irrelevant perturbations (C78-C89), while peer R4 focuses on the theoretical significance of task-irrelevant perturbations causing task-relevant errors (C85-C93, C116, C146, C155). Both find evidence convincing but peer reviewers request more discussion of underlying mechanisms.

Partial overlap on Experiment 2 error findings. OpenEval R7 addresses end-effector relevant errors from irrelevant adaptation (C90-C94, C155-C158) with detailed statistical support. Peer R4 acknowledges this as an important novel finding but requests more theoretical discussion of why adaptation occurs and how internal models explain it.

Both address synthesis of dual mechanisms (C95, C116). OpenEval finds the synthesis logical and well-supported by experimental data. Peer reviewers accept this as valuable theoretical contribution showing how baseline relationships determine learning, with editor confirming evidence is convincing.

Both address mechanistic interpretations (C146-C149, C163-C168). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are explicitly speculative and not directly tested. Peer reviewers similarly express uncertainty, requesting extended discussion of how internal models may explain the findings, particularly for end-effector irrelevant perturbations.

Both address implicit adaptation claims (C76-C77, C144). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are explicitly labeled as speculation by authors. Peer Reviewer 1 questions whether evidence supports exclusive implicit control and suggests removing 'implicit' from title/abstract, indicating similar uncertainty about this interpretation.

Both address gradual vs. abrupt perturbation comparison (C73-C75). OpenEval finds the control data appropriately documented despite smaller sample size in abrupt condition. Peer Reviewer 1 notes 'there is no clear comparison between gradual and abrupt sessions,' suggesting the comparison could be strengthened.

Both address minimal intervention principle interpretation (C67, C139-C140, C147, C163-C168). OpenEval notes conflicting interpretations within the manuscript (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers request more discussion of why both perturbation types drive adaptation and how this relates to internal model predictions.

Both address generalizability limitations (C113). OpenEval finds the acknowledgment appropriate given the specific configuration tested (SUPPORTED). Peer Reviewer 3 and editor explicitly raise concerns about limited generalizability, requesting future work examining different configurations (UNCERTAIN).

Minimal overlap. OpenEval R13 addresses extensive background and novelty claims (C1-C36, C107-C128), finding them well-supported. Peer R1 focuses on task design praise but shares only C127 regarding novelty. Both find the conceptual framework and task innovation well-established.

OpenEval R9 addresses Experiment 3 design and predictions (C96-C100, C193-C195), finding them logically derived and clearly stated. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the experimental design rationale, though peer reviewers accepted the results (see peer R6).

OpenEval R15 addresses literature contextualization (C133-C135, C141-C143), finding comparisons to prior work appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these literature comparisons.

OpenEval R17 addresses distinction from previous 'task-irrelevant' work (C150-C154), finding the conceptual clarification important and well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this distinction, though it relates to the novelty praised in peer R1.

OpenEval R18 addresses Experiment 3 interpretations about interaction and dual optimization (C159, C161-C162), finding them logical though interpretive. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these Experiment 3 interpretations.

OpenEval R19 addresses data analysis methods (C196-C202), finding them appropriate with minor suggestions for more detail on multiple comparisons. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses methodological details.
